title: I Am a Stranger Living with You — Weeping, a Purchase, a Cave
blocks: Brothers and sisters, peace be with you. Last lesson we stood on Mount Moriah and saw a knife held back and a ram caught in a thicket. Today the camera comes down off that mountain — and the moment it reaches the bottom, we are standing at a funeral.
Verse 1: "Sarah lived one hundred twenty-seven years. This was the length of Sarah's life."

Brothers and sisters, this is the only time in the whole Old Testament that a woman's age is written down. The author records her years, her death and her burial place at full patriarchal scale. She is not the scenery. She is a party to the covenant.
And the question this lesson puts to us is this: if God had promised you an entire land, and you still had to pay money for one cave in which to bury your wife, what would you make of that?

Let me give you the answer up front: only a person who knows he has a home dares to admit that where he is now he is a guest. And all this man ever received was one cave — and that cave was the first stake he drove into the land of promise.
Verse 2: "Sarah died in Kiriath Arba (also called Hebron), in the land of Canaan. Abraham came to mourn for Sarah, and to weep for her."
Brothers and sisters, stop at that sentence.

This is the man who laid his only son on an altar on Mount Moriah. This is the man who heard God speak and set out, and who kept walking for more than sixty years. And now he is sitting beside his wife's body, mourning and weeping.

The Hebrew uses two verbs here. "To mourn", לִסְפֹּד, is the formal rite of lamentation; "to weep for her", וְלִבְכֹּתָהּ, is the shedding of tears. One is the ceremony on the outside; the other is the tears on the inside.
Scripture nowhere asks a person of faith not to cry.

I want to say one thing especially to those brothers and sisters who are in the middle of losing someone. If anyone tells you, "Be strong, don't cry", that is not the teaching of the Bible. John 11:35, the shortest verse in the whole Bible, says, "Jesus wept." And when he wept, he knew perfectly well that four minutes later he was going to call Lazarus out of that tomb.
He knew the ending, and he wept anyway.

And verse 3 says, "Abraham rose up from before his dead." Brothers and sisters — first weep, then rise. That order cannot be reversed, and neither step can be left out. Some people have only verse 2: they sink into it and never get up again. Some people skip verse 2 and force themselves upright — and the grief they never finished crying will come up years later, out of somewhere else entirely.
"Abraham came to mourn for Sarah, and to weep for her" — does a father of faith really still weep like that?

He does, and Scripture wrote it down. Verse 2 uses two verbs: "mourn" (סָפַד, the public rite of lamentation) and "weep" (בָּכָה, to shed tears). Which is to say: he did the ceremony that had to be done, and he also genuinely cried. This verse matters, because a great many Christians have been taught that "people with hope shouldn't grieve too much." That is not what the Bible says. The Lord Jesus wept at Lazarus' tomb, and Paul says that we do not "grieve like the rest, who have no hope" — what he says is not like them; he does not say do not grieve. So if you are in the middle of a loss, you may cry. Crying is not a shortage of faith. Crying is the evidence of love.
Sarah's age is specially recorded. Is that a common thing in the Bible?

No, it is not. Verse 1 says, "Sarah lived one hundred twenty-seven years" — she is the only woman in the whole Bible whose lifespan is explicitly written down. That is how the text pays her its respect: she is not somebody's appendage, she is a person of weight. In the literature of that age this is highly unusual. And the reminder for us today is very practical: the way a church remembers a person reflects the way we actually regard that person in our hearts. There is a small thing you can do about it — at a memorial service, or at a family remembrance, say the names and tell the stories of the sisters, of the older members, of the people who served quietly, and do not leave someone with nothing but the phrase "so-and-so's wife."
2. A Light from the Original: I Am a Stranger and a Foreigner
Verse 4: "I am a stranger and a foreigner living with you. Give me a possession of a burying-place with you, that I may bury my dead out of my sight."

Brothers and sisters, "stranger" is גֵּר (*ger*) and "foreigner" is תּוֹשָׁב (*toshav*), and in law those two words carry a very concrete meaning: he holds none of the land rights a native holds, so he cannot buy land on his own — it has to go through the consent of the elders of the city.
So the first layer of meaning is legal: he genuinely was not qualified.

But the second layer weighs more. He had lived in this land for sixty-two years. He had hundreds of servants; he had beaten a coalition of four kings; he was one of the richest men in the region; and the children of Heth called him "a prince of God among us" — in the original נְשִׂיא אֱלֹהִים, literally "a chief of God", the highest title of honour they had to give.
A man who had lived there sixty-two years, a man the local people honoured like that — and the first sentence out of his mouth is: I am a stranger and a foreigner living with you.
That is not low self-esteem. That is knowing where he stands.

And Hebrews 11:13 catches that sentence as it falls: "These all died in faith, not having received the promises, but having seen them and embraced them from afar, and having confessed that they were strangers and pilgrims on the earth." And verse 16 says, "But now they desire a better country, that is, a heavenly one."
Brothers and sisters, follow the logic of that: he dared to admit that here he was a guest, because he knew that somewhere else there was a home.

A man with no home does not dare admit he is a guest — he will work himself half to death decorating the hotel room until it looks like a house. And that is exactly how a great many of us are living: because we are not certain in our hearts whether there is an eternal home, we grab at everything here.
"I am a stranger and a foreigner living with you" — hadn't he already been living there for over sixty years?

Over sixty years, and this is still what he calls himself. The two words in the original carry real weight: גֵּר (a stranger) and תּוֹשָׁב (a foreigner). And Hebrews 11 lifts the whole matter higher: they "confessed that they were strangers and pilgrims on the earth … But now they desire a better country, that is, a heavenly one." So this is not low self-esteem; it is clarity about identity. The thing to be careful of is reading it as "therefore I need not fit in and I need not invest" — in fact he dealt with the local people, negotiated with them and kept every courtesy. The right shape of it is this: live here wholly, and do not treat here as the destination. And the practical test is this: would you let go of the things that only count in heaven in order to stand more securely here?
From verse 5 on comes a stretch of very Eastern negotiation. If you have ever bought anything in a market, it will feel familiar.
The children of Heth say, "You are a prince of God among us. Bury your dead in the best of our tombs." It sounds enormously generous — but that is the offer of a loan, not the offer of a gift.

Abraham rose up and bowed himself down to them. Verse 7 and verse 12 — twice in this one chapter he bows. Brothers and sisters, he bows to the men he is about to do business with. That is the breeding of a great man.
Then he says what he actually wants: "Hear me, and entreat for me to Ephron the son of Zohar, that he may sell me the cave of Machpelah, which he has, which is in the end of his field."

Notice two details. First, what he asks for is the cave "in the end of his field", בִּקְצֵה שָׂדֵהוּ — the piece at the far edge of the land, so as not to take the good ground from the man. Second, the moment he opens his mouth he says, "For the full price let him sell it to me", בְּכֶסֶף מָלֵא (*bechesef male*) — silver in full measure, the whole price.
And Ephron's reply is a classic of Eastern bargaining: "No, my lord, hear me. I give you the field, and I give you the cave that is in it."
Brothers and sisters, that sounds magnificently open-handed — and then the next thing he says is, "What is a piece of land worth four hundred shekels of silver between me and you?"

First he says "I give it to you", and then, in the lightest possible brushstroke, he names a staggering figure. What sort of sum is four hundred shekels? Jeremiah bought a field for seventeen shekels. David paid fifty shekels for a threshing floor.

And what did Abraham do? He did not so much as counter-offer. Verse 16: "Abraham listened to Ephron. Abraham weighed to Ephron the silver which he had named in the hearing of the children of Heth, four hundred shekels of silver, according to the current merchants' standard."
Brothers and sisters, why did he not haggle? Because what he was buying was not land. He was buying a title that could never be reopened.

Verses 17 to 20 use the standard language of an ancient deed of sale: the field, the cave that was in it, and all the trees within its borders "were deeded to Abraham for a possession in the presence of the children of Heth, before all who went in at the gate of his city." Boundaries, trees, witnesses, purchase price — the whole instrument, complete.
This is the only property he ever owned in the land of promise.
The children of Heth offered to give it to him for nothing. Why did he insist on paying?

Because a gift can be taken back, and only what is bought is property. That is very practical wisdom. An arrangement built on goodwill can be reopened later; a transaction completed by the rules stands there in black and white. The text is written with extreme care — at the gate of the city, in front of the local people, four hundred shekels weighed out "according to the current merchants' standard." And he was not only protecting himself; he was driving a stake in for the generations that came after him. The reminder for us today is this: where money, property or responsibility is involved, complete it properly — even when it is your own family, even when the other side is being gracious. Being clear is not the same as being distrustful. Being clear is how you protect the relationship.
Was four hundred shekels simply an outsider being fleeced?

Some commentators think the price was on the high side — in Jeremiah 32 Jeremiah buys a field for seventeen shekels, and in 2 Samuel 24 David pays fifty shekels for a threshing floor. Others point out that this purchase covered a whole field along with the trees in it, and that different periods and different locations cannot be compared directly anyway. The text itself passes no comment, so we need not deliver a verdict on its behalf. What is certain is this: he did not beat the price down, and he did not complain. There are times when getting a thing done cleanly matters more than the money you might have saved — and that is especially so when the thing is going to be left to the next generation.
4. A Stake Driven into the Land of Promise
Brothers and sisters, I want you to look at what became of that cave.

Genesis 25:9 — Abraham is buried there. Genesis 49:31 — Jacob, at the end of his life, gives this instruction: "There they buried Abraham and Sarah, his wife. There they buried Isaac and Rebekah, his wife, and there I buried Leah." And Genesis 50:13 — Jacob himself is buried there too.
Six people. Four generations. One cave.

And look at Genesis 49:29–30, at the thing Jacob cared about most at the end. He had lived seventeen good years in Egypt; his son was prime minister; the whole household was clothed and fed. And what he spends his last breath on is this — do not bury me here; carry me back to the cave of Machpelah.
And in Genesis 50:25 Joseph goes further still: he hands his own bones over to people who would not be born for another four hundred years.
Brothers and sisters, that cave became a direction. With their own bones they pinned down the promise of God.
"I do not belong to Egypt. I am going back."
And the beginning of all of it is an old man of a hundred and thirty-seven, on the day his wife died, paying a staggering price for the far corner of somebody else's field.

At the time nobody could see what that money was worth. The children of Heth probably thought him a fool; Ephron probably thought he had done rather well out of it. And three thousand years later that cave is still in Hebron — and the line that started there ran all the way to Bethlehem.
Brothers and sisters, this is what faith looks like: you drive in first a stake whose value nobody else can see.
What kind of estate is one burial cave? God promised the whole land.

It is precisely because it was the only piece that faith shows up in it. He never received that land in his lifetime, and yet he bought a cave to bury people in — a stake driven into the land of promise, which is a way of saying with his hands: I believe my descendants are going to live here. And that cave went on to become the family burial ground: Abraham, Sarah, Isaac, Rebekah, Jacob and Leah were all buried there (Genesis 49:31). So it is not a small plot of land; it is a declaration that reaches across four generations. And the lesson for us is this: you may not see in your lifetime the thing you have been asking for, but you can do one concrete thing that points towards it.
5. Distortions You Must Be Able to Spot

The first is turning the purchase of this field into a lesson on money management. There are preachers who handle this chapter by saying "buy property" and "make provision for your family" — those are not bad pieces of advice, but they are not this chapter. The centre of gravity in chapter 23 is "I am a foreigner" and that city with foundations. When the congregation walks out, what they should be valuing is the city, not the portfolio.

The second is pushing "he did not haggle" into a rule that a Christian may never negotiate. The same man, in chapter 18, bargained all the way down to ten for the sake of Sodom. Where is the difference? For other people's sake you may argue; for your own advantage you may yield. Flatten it into a blanket rule and you will raise a roomful of people who dare not handle anything, and who call their avoidance spirituality.

The third is preaching "we are pilgrims" as though it excused us from making a decent job of the life we have now. Look how carefully this man works in this chapter: the whole procedure walked through, in front of everyone, silver by the merchants' standard, boundaries and trees written out one by one. A pilgrim's heart does not mean a careless pair of hands. First Peter 2:11 calls us foreigners and pilgrims; verse 12 of that same letter says we are to have "good behavior among the nations."

The fourth is passing over Abraham's weeping. Verse 2 says he mourned and he wept. Skip it, and the brothers and sisters in the room who are grieving will conclude that their tears are proof of their weakness.

The fifth is preaching this chapter as a piece of connective tissue with no message in it. I know that a land purchase is hard to make dramatic. But dispose of it in two minutes and what the congregation learns is that "there are parts of the Bible you can skip." And in fact this chapter is one of the coordinates of the whole Bible: it tells you that sixty-two years can stand between a promise and its fulfilment — and that faith is what buys a cave inside that gap.
6. Two Real Questions from a Chinese Setting

The first question: Chinese families take funerals and geomancy extremely seriously, and when there is a death in the house the relatives often ask us to take part in things we cannot take part in. What do we do? Brothers and sisters, this chapter gives us several very practical directions. First, face the grief squarely. Abraham mourned and wept, and Scripture never asked him to be strong. A Christian funeral is not a funeral without tears; it is a funeral where we do not "grieve like the rest, who have no hope." Second, separate filial duty from worship. In this chapter Abraham did everything that ought to be done — the formal mourning, a dignified burial, the legal procedure, a generous price. He was discharging the responsibility that was his to discharge. What he did not do was hand worship over to another object. That distinction is intensely practical: with the arrangements, the courtesies and the ceremonies, comply as far as you can; on the object of worship, you cannot give way. Third — and this is the most practical of all — do not start a war at a funeral. Most conflicts with relatives are not theological problems; they are communication problems. Talk with the senior members of the family beforehand, explain what you will do and what you will not do, and take on more of the labour and more of the cost yourself. Abraham paid the full price, and he bowed to the children of Heth twice.

The second question: I have lived far from home for years — as an immigrant, on a posting, as a student — and I often feel that I do not belong anywhere. What does this chapter say to me? Brothers and sisters, this chapter may well have been written for you. First, "a stranger and a foreigner" is not a condition to be shaken off as fast as possible; it is Scripture's formal title for the children of God. Your unsettledness is not a failure. It is a kind of clear-sightedness. Second, notice how he goes about being a pilgrim: he lived in earnest, he built relationships in earnest, he handled his affairs in earnest, and in earnest he bought a piece of land. Being a pilgrim is not the same as not investing. Third — and this is the one that matters most — he dared to admit he was a guest because he knew there was a home somewhere else. If you find yourself abroad and straining to prove that "I belong here too", that strain may not be a problem of cultural adjustment at all; it may be that the place of home in your heart has not yet settled. Hebrews 11:16 says, "Therefore God is not ashamed of them, to be called their God, for he has prepared a city for them."
An older relative in the family has died. How do I handle the tension between the traditions of the funeral and my faith?

Settle three principles first. One, respect: Abraham "bowed himself down" before the children of Heth and did things according to the local courtesies; he did not despise other people's customs because his faith was different. Two, boundaries: whatever you can take part in — being present, bowing, helping, looking after the relatives — take part in as fully as you can; where the worship of other gods is involved, explain honestly and decline, and keep the tone gentle, and say it in advance rather than refusing in front of everyone on the day. Three, timing: do not argue principles when feeling is running highest. Serve first, be present first, and explain once the relationship is steady. And most important of all: what the family will remember is usually not the reasoning you gave them. It is whether you showed up during those few days.
7. Living 321 Out — Drive That Stake in First
Brothers and sisters, let us tie this lesson back into the Three Foundations, the Two Core Values and the Goal of 321.

Jesus is my role model — verse 3 says, "Abraham rose up from before his dead." First weep, then rise. And in John 11 the Lord Jesus wept at Lazarus' tomb, and then he said, "Lazarus, come out!" Brothers and sisters, this is my role model: he weeps alongside us, and he also raises us up. So when we go to comfort a bereaved family, the first thing to do is to sit down and weep with them, not to hurry in with our explanations.

The Bible is my standard — and the standard this chapter hands us is an identity: I am a foreigner here. That identity will shape every financial decision you make, every reaction you have to gain and to loss, the temperature of every argument you get into. A man who knows he is a guest has a great deal less energy left over for keeping score.

The Holy Spirit is my guide — notice how steady this man is. He has just lost the wife who was at his side for decades, and he can still walk an exacting legal procedure through from beginning to end. Brothers and sisters, that is not cold-bloodedness. That is what a person looks like when God is holding him steady. Psalm 23 says, "He restores my soul", and that restoring very often happens on precisely the days when we have to weep and handle business at the same time.

Let Jesus be King — "I am a stranger and a foreigner living with you." Once you admit you are a pilgrim, you no longer have to fight to the death over one piece of ground. To let Jesus be King is to re-order the list of things I absolutely must hold on to. Brothers and sisters, if the one thing in your life you will not loosen your grip on is a thing you cannot take with you, then it has no business standing first on that list.

Let Jesus receive all the glory — there is no miracle in this chapter, no vision, and God does not speak once. It is simply a man conducting himself honestly through a funeral. And God's name is still there in it — the children of Heth call him "a prince of God." Sometimes God is glorified not by a meeting but by a funeral carried out with dignity and honesty.

Establish God's system — that cave went on to hold four generations. Brothers and sisters, one small plot of land bought by one man became the root of a nation. To establish God's system is to drive in first the stake whose value nobody else can see: the family altar you begin today, that small group, that notebook you are keeping for your children — none of it looks like anything now. Thirty years from now somebody will be standing there.

And here I want to say something honest about 321 itself. We put a great deal of weight on "receiving", on "inheriting", on "entering into destiny" — and this chapter supplies a very heavy counterweight: the man who inherited the whole land of promise bought exactly one cave in his lifetime. Hebrews 11 says plainly that they died "not having received the promises." So when we teach, we have to give people two things at the same time: confidence in the promises of God, and preparation for the possibility of not seeing them honoured within this life. Give them only the first, and the congregation will collapse at the first month when nothing comes through.
8. Four Kinds of Heart, One Cave
Brothers and sisters, the same cave of Machpelah, falling into four kinds of heart, gives four different things to look at.

The proud heart says, "All that money, and he didn't even own a field?" This heart measures a person's spiritual life by his estate. Brothers and sisters, notice what the text calls him: the children of Heth call him "a prince of God." His weight was never on a title deed. And Luke 12:15 says that "a man's life doesn't consist of the abundance of the things which he possesses."

The fearful heart says, "Then am I going to leave nothing at all behind me?" This heart is terrified of having lived for nothing. To that heart I want to say: look at what became of that cave. All he left at the time was a cave — and that cave became the direction in which four generations came home. The one small thing you do today may be exactly that stake.

The ashamed heart says, "Wherever I go, I am the outsider." It may be your accent, your schooling, your family background, or something in your past that leaves you feeling in every group that you do not quite belong. Brothers and sisters, look carefully: "a stranger and a foreigner" is the formal title this father of faith gave himself, and Hebrews turned it into a commendation of every believer. The way you do not fit may not be a defect at all. It may be a mark.

The wounded heart says, "I have just lost someone." This chapter is for you. It offers no arguments; it records one thing only: he wept, and then he rose, and then he carefully finished the business that had to be finished. Brothers and sisters, if all you can manage right now is the first of those, that is enough. Scripture gives you permission to stay in verse 2.
9. This Week, a Few Things You Can Do

First, give yourself permission to cry once. If there is a loss inside you that you have never finished crying over — a person, a relationship, a hope that never came true — give it some time this week. The order in the text is: weep first, then rise.

Second, write down three things you cannot take with you. Just three of the things you are gripping most tightly at the moment. Look at the list when you have finished it, and then say one sentence to God: I cannot take these with me.

Third, drive in a stake. Do one thing whose value will not show for thirty years — write down your testimony and leave it for your children, begin praying regularly for one member of your family, put one broken relationship back together.

Fourth, do one piece of business honestly and properly. There is something this week where you could cut a corner, or where you could come out a little ahead at somebody else's expense — pay the full price, walk the whole procedure, do it in front of everyone. Abraham did not even counter-offer.

Fifth, this week tell this lesson to one friend outside the church in three sentences: there is a man in the Bible to whom God promised an entire land, and he lived there sixty-two years and only bought a burial plot, at a staggering price, on the day his wife died; the first thing he said to the local people was, "I am a stranger and a foreigner living with you"; and the Bible later explains that he dared to admit he was a guest because he knew there was a city somewhere else.
Brothers and sisters, let us declare together before God:
I declare that I am a stranger and a pilgrim on this earth; none of this goes with me.
I declare that I dare to admit that I am a guest here, because I know there is a home somewhere else.
I declare that a pilgrim's heart does not mean a careless pair of hands; I will do the work in my hands honestly and properly.
I declare that I will drive in the stake whose value nobody else can see, even if I never live to sit in its shade.
This week I am to "drive in a stake that points to the future" — what could that actually be?

Here are some very practical options. One: write something down for the next generation — a letter, a testimony, a piece of your family's faith story. Two: do something whose results you will not see now — begin praying regularly for one particular person, begin setting aside money with a purpose attached to it, begin raising up someone to take the baton from you. Three: put one decision in black and white — the proportion you give, a will, a directive about medical care. None of that is romantic, but all of it has the shape of buying a piece of land. Choose one thing you can genuinely finish this week, and tell one person, so that he can come back and ask you about it. And one reminder: you do not have to wait until "the time is right." The day Abraham bought that field was the hardest day of his life.
Brothers and sisters, if only one picture from this lesson may remain, let it be an old man standing at the edge of a field, counting out silver.

He is a hundred and thirty-seven. His wife has just died. He has lived on this land for sixty-two years, and four times God has said to him, I will give this land to your offspring. And now he stands at the gate of a Hittite city, in front of everyone, and by the merchants' standard weight he weighs out four hundred shekels of silver for the far corner of a field and one cave inside it.
From a human point of view it is a terrible piece of business — paying a high price for the very thing that had already been promised to him.
But brothers and sisters, he is not buying land. He is driving in a stake.

He is saying: I believe this land belongs to my descendants. I cannot afford the whole of it yet, so I will begin with one cave. I will bury Sarah here, and I will be buried here myself, and my son and my grandsons will be buried here too. Because this is our home.
Three thousand years have gone by. That cave is still in Hebron.
And Hebrews 11 says that what they desired was a better country, a heavenly one — and that "God is not ashamed of them, to be called their God, for he has prepared a city for them."
Brothers and sisters, all he bought in a lifetime was one cave. And what God prepared for him was a city.

The focus is not on how much I own in this life, not on what I leave behind me, and not on feeling like an outsider wherever I go. The focus is on Jesus — he said, "I am going to prepare a place for you." Not I, but Christ.

May God bless every one of us this week: to weep once, honestly; then to rise and do well the work that is in our hands; and to drive in that stake. In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray, amen.

Leader's note: the Three Transformations are one road running downward. The first drives the point into the head; the second carries it from the head into the heart; the third carries it from the heart into the days of the week. If time runs short, cover fewer questions rather than skipping the third — without reaching the third transformation, this lesson stops at a mindset.

Priority markers: ★★★ = highest priority; if time is short, discuss at least this one in each transformation. ★★ = second priority. ★ = if time allows. The multiplication assignment marked [Must do] may not be dropped; it can be finished at home.
Transformation One | Internalise — until it becomes mindset (about 20 minutes)
Purpose: through discussion, to drive the point of this lesson into a clear mindset.
1. ★★ "I am a stranger and a foreigner living with you" — sixty years in, and he still says it. Is that low self-esteem, or is that clarity?
2. ★★★ They offered to give it to him for nothing, and he insisted on paying. How does that insistence apply today — in a family, in a church, at work?
3. ★ Abraham both mourned and wept. What correction does that make to the idea of whether a Christian ought to grieve?
4. ★★ In a whole lifetime he bought one burial cave. How does that help us understand what it means to act before you can see anything?
Leader's reminder: the aim of this section is that people can say it, not that they answer beautifully. If someone is speaking in fragments, help him tidy it up; do not finish his sentence for him.
Transformation Two | Digest — until it becomes life (about 35 minutes · the heart of this lesson)
Purpose: through seeing, listening, thinking, speaking and doing, to digest the mindset until it becomes life.

5. ★★★ The manuscript named four kinds of heart — proud (I don't need to lean on anybody's goodwill), fearful (if I lose this I won't hold up), ashamed (I have been crying far too long), wounded (someone said the wrong thing to me when I was in the most pain). Which are you most like? What experience made you that way?
6. ★★ Read aloud: "I am a stranger and a foreigner living with you." Then tell the group: where does that sentence touch you?
7. ★★ Is there a loss inside you that you have never finished crying over? You do not have to give the details. Only say this: at the time, what was it that stopped you crying?
8. ★ Finish this in one sentence: "The thing I most want to leave to the next generation is …"
9. ★★ Which stake pointing to the future will you drive in this week? Name the thing, and name the day you will have it finished.

Leader's reminder: this lesson will touch the pain of bereavement. If someone is in the middle of grief, stay with him first; do not hurry in with hope, and do not say things like "he has gone to a better place." Give him time, and follow up with him privately after the meeting.
Transformation Three | Transform — until it becomes daily living (about 25 minutes)
Purpose: through discussing concrete application, to transform life into daily living.
10. ★★ Is there something in your wider family this week that ought to be settled properly, by the rules? Say how you are going to open the conversation.
11. ★ The same question in another setting: at work or in your service, what is being held together by unspoken understanding when it ought to be written down?
12. ★★★ The writing practice: this week write a short letter to the next generation, or write down a piece of your own faith story. Say who you are writing to, and when you will write it.
13. ★★ The 920 practice: find your one "2" — your spiritual companion — tell him about the stake you are going to drive in, and ask him to check on you on the day you named. Say his name now.

14. ★★★ [Must do] Multiplication assignment: this week, tell this lesson to one friend outside the church in three sentences. First, there is a man in the Bible who was promised a whole land and bought exactly one burial cave in his lifetime. Second, they offered it to him for nothing and he insisted on paying the price, settling it properly in front of the whole city. Third, so what I learned is that some things have to be done cleanly, because they are being left to the next generation. Write down now who you will tell.

In pairs, tell each other two things: the stake you are driving in this week, and the matter you are going to settle properly. Then pray for each other, asking the Lord that in the days of our sojourning on the earth we may be able both to keep going and to let go.
